subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Look at the map for the southernmost point of India (p. 95)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map showing Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Indira Point (p. 95)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 95 and asks students what they notice about land surrounded by water on all sides. Students share ideas freely while the teacher records key words on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 95 and study the map carefully. They locate the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, trace the coastline to find Indira Point, and record in their notebooks: the name of the sea in which the islands sit, any other islands they can spot or name, and what 'southernmost tip' means for India's shape.

In pairs, students share their findings and together write one sentence explaining why Indira Point is significant. Pairs then compare their lists of other islands they know, and the teacher invites two or three pairs to share with the class, building a collective list on the board.

Students sketch a quick outline of the region from the map, mark the islands, and write one observation about what makes an island different from a peninsula. Teacher asks: 'If you lived on an island, what would be different about your daily life?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a country-level map to locate and describe the position of natural geographic features.
periods.section_context: India map, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Indira Point, Bay of Bengal, island definition, other islands of India.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'How does the sea around an island shape the lives of the people who live there?' Prompt those who finish quickly to count approximately how many islands appear on the map and consider what 'over a thousand islands' really means.

periods.activity_title: Buttress Root Model — How Roots Hold Trees
periods.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Roll newspaper into a thin tube, make it stand, then add paper triangles around the base and test stability again (p. 96)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of buttress roots and paper-tube activity steps (p. 96)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 96 and shows the illustration of buttress roots. Students observe the roots' shape and the teacher poses the question: 'What problem do you think these wide, flaring roots are solving for the tree?' Students predict in one sentence in their notebooks.

Students follow the steps in Textbook p. 96: roll a sheet of newspaper into a tight tube, glue the edge, and stand it on the desk. They record whether it stays upright. They then cut three or four small triangles from thick paper, attach them evenly around the base of the tube, and test again, recording what changes and writing a sentence explaining why.

Groups of three compare results and agree on one explanation linking the triangle supports to the shape of buttress roots in island forests. A spokesperson from each group shares their explanation with the class while the teacher lists the key ideas on the board without confirming or correcting immediately.

Teacher leads a brief whole-class discussion consolidating the structural principle: wider base, more stability. Students write a closing sentence in their notebooks connecting the paper-tube model to what buttress roots do for tall trees in waterlogged forest soil.

periods.implied_lo: Students can test a structural hypothesis using a physical model and connect the result to a natural engineering principle.
periods.section_context: Newspaper tube model, triangular paper supports, buttress roots, tall trees in island forest, stability testing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What would happen to a tall tree in wet, muddy soil if its roots only went straight down?' Ensure each student individually records a prediction before the group stage so every voice is committed to paper first.

periods.activity_title: Sea Life Discussion — Coral Reefs and Ocean Interdependence
periods.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Discuss how the coral reef helps fish and other sea creatures (p. 98)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of coral reef and marine life near Andaman and Nicobar Islands (p. 97–98)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook pp. 97–98 and spend a quiet moment listing in their notebooks at least three living things found in the sea, drawing on the images and any prior knowledge. Teacher asks them not to look at a neighbour's list yet.

Students draw or write about one favourite sea animal, noting where it lives and what it eats. Teacher then opens a whole-class share: pairs of students read their choices aloud. The teacher groups responses on the board by habitat — open water, reef, sea floor.

Class discusses two questions from Textbook p. 98: 'Why is life under the sea as important as life in forests?' and 'How does a coral reef help fish and other sea creatures?' Students contribute ideas while the teacher maps connections between species on the board — who shelters whom, who feeds on whom.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one on what a coral reef does for the creatures around it, and one connecting this to a question about the North Sentinel Islanders' knowledge of the sea and whether deep familiarity with nature could help people stay safe. Teacher closes by asking: 'What might you notice about the sea if you lived beside it your whole life?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe interdependence within a marine ecosystem and explain why protecting it matters.
periods.section_context: Coral reef, Marine Interpretation Centre, dolphin, fish, sea creatures, Andaman and Nicobar marine biodiversity, North Sentinel Island people, nature-reading knowledge.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When discussing the North Sentinel Islanders, invite students to consider what kinds of knowledge get passed down through generations of living close to the sea — without introducing the word 'knowledge systems'. Ask: 'What would you notice if your family had lived by the same shore for hundreds of years?'

periods.activity_title: Mangrove Roots — What Makes the Sundarbans Different
periods.textbook_anchor: Sundarbans: Home of the Mangroves — Write what you find in the mangrove forest and what makes this place different from other forests (p. 99)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of mangrove roots, aerial roots, and Sundarbans landscape (p. 99–100)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 99 and asks students to look closely at the image of mangrove roots. Students spend time observing silently, then write in their notebooks: what they see that looks different from a regular forest, and any questions the image raises for them.

Students write their responses to the two tasks from Textbook p. 99: listing at least three things found in the mangrove forest, and writing what they think makes the Sundarbans different from other forests. Teacher circulates and reads responses without commenting, noting recurring ideas to draw out in discussion.

Teacher leads a structured observation discussion: What do the roots look like? Why are some roots above the ground? What happens when the tide comes in? Students connect the two root types — aerial breathing roots and soil-holding roots — to the specific challenge of living in salty, waterlogged land. Teacher draws a simple labelled sketch on the board.

Students add labels to a sketch of mangrove roots in their notebooks and write one sentence explaining how each root type helps the tree survive. Teacher closes with: 'What would happen to the coastline if the mangrove roots disappeared?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe structural features of plants and explain how those features help the plant survive in its specific habitat.
periods.section_context: Sundarbans, mangrove forest, aerial breathing roots, soil-holding roots, salty waterlogged land, coastline protection, Ganga meets the sea.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you know any other plant that has a special trick for surviving in a difficult place?' This opens space for students to connect mangrove roots to their own local observations. If students mention local water plants or trees, draw the parallel briefly without digressing.

periods.activity_title: People of the Sundarbans — Living with the Forest
periods.textbook_anchor: Sundarbans: Home of the Mangroves — In what ways do people in Sunderbans depend on the mangrove forests? (p. 100)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of honey collectors and Sundarbans community life (p. 100–101)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook pp. 100–101 and invites students to read the section on how people live in the Sundarbans. Students read quietly and underline or circle anything that surprises them.

Students write their response to the task on Textbook p. 100: in what ways do people in the Sundarbans depend on mangrove forests? Teacher asks them to think about food, work, shelter, and protection. After writing, students share in pairs, adding to each other's lists.

Whole-class discussion on the tiger-mask tradition used by honey collectors. Teacher asks: 'What problem were the honey collectors trying to solve? What does wearing a mask on the back of the head tell us about how carefully these people had observed tiger behaviour?' Students connect this to the idea of knowledge built through long observation.

Students discuss from Textbook p. 101 why it is important to take care of places like the Sundarbans, then each writes one sentence on why protecting the forest also protects the people who live in it. Teacher closes: 'If the mangroves were cut down, who or what would be affected first?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how a community's way of life is shaped by and dependent on a specific natural ecosystem.
periods.section_context: Sundarbans community dependence, honey collectors, tiger-mask tradition, mangrove forest livelihood, generational living with forest, coastline protection for villages.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When discussing the honey collectors' tiger-mask tradition, ask: 'How long do you think it took people to figure out that tigers always attack from behind? What does that tell us about how they learned?' This surfaces the depth of observation behind traditional practices without labelling it.

periods.activity_title: Northeast India — Reading the Region Through Pictures
periods.section_ref: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions — Look at the picture and identify three things being sold in the market (p. 102)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of Northeast India market, festival, bamboo houses, and animals (p. 102)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 102 and look at the full set of images in silence. Teacher asks: 'Before you read the text, what can you already tell me about this region just from the pictures?' Students write three observations in their notebooks.

Students work through the observation tasks from Textbook p. 102: identifying three things sold in the market, naming the festival shown, explaining why houses are built on bamboo structures, naming animals in the image, and writing what the pictures tell them about how people in Northeast India live with nature. Each answer goes into their notebooks.

Small groups of three share their answers and discuss any differences. Teacher invites groups to share their response to the last question — what the pictures tell them about people living with nature — and builds a class list of observations on the board, grouping them into: landscape, food and markets, festivals, shelter, and wildlife.

Teacher reads aloud a brief section of the text describing the Seven Sisters and Sikkim's forests and traditions, and students add one new fact they did not get from the images alone to their notebooks. Teacher asks: 'What would you want to find out about this region that the pictures cannot tell you?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can read visual sources to identify features of a region's natural environment and cultural life, and articulate what the images reveal about human-nature relationships.
periods.section_context: Northeast India, Seven Sisters states, Sikkim, market goods, festival, bamboo houses, animals, forests, rivers, cultural traditions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think bamboo is a good material for building houses in this region?' Let students reason from what they can see — forest availability, flexibility, ease of building — before adding any explanation. This keeps observation primary.

periods.activity_title: Bird Nest Build — The Hargila Conservation Story
periods.section_ref: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions — Collect twigs, leaves, and soft materials; create a small bird's nest and consider what makes a good nest (p. 104)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the Hargila (Greater Adjutant Stork) and its nesting habitat (p. 104)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud or paraphrases the Hargila conservation story from the text — how women in a community began teaching children to protect stork nests. Teacher opens Textbook p. 104 and shows the image. Students discuss briefly: 'What does a nest need to do? What problems does it have to solve?'

In groups of three or four, students collect materials available in the classroom (twigs, leaves, cotton, paper strips) and build a small bird's nest following the task from Textbook p. 104. As they build, they record in their notebooks: what materials they chose, why, and what challenge they ran into. They also write answers to 'What makes a good nest?' and 'What does the nest need to keep eggs safe?'

Groups place their nests on the desk and do a gallery walk to observe other groups' designs. Each group writes one thing another group did that they had not thought of. Teacher asks: 'Which nest do you think would survive a rainstorm? Why?'

Brief whole-class close: Teacher connects nest-building back to the Hargila story — 'The women who protect these nests understand exactly what the birds need. How does that knowledge come from?' Students share one-word or one-phrase answers aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design a simple structure to meet specific natural requirements and connect the design process to the way communities observe and protect wildlife.
periods.section_context: Hargila (Greater Adjutant Stork), bird nest construction, twigs, leaves, cotton and soft materials, community conservation by women, Northeast India forest.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: While groups build, circulate and ask: 'Why did you choose that material?' and 'What would happen to the eggs if the nest tipped?' This keeps the inquiry grounded in function rather than appearance. If a group finishes quickly, prompt them to test their nest by placing a small pebble in it.

periods.activity_title: Root Bridge Challenge — Engineering with Nature
periods.section_ref: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions — Connect two chairs using string or sticks in a way that will hold a small toy (p. 105)
materials: small toy or eraser (as test weight)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image or description of living root bridges of Meghalaya (p. 105)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 105 and discusses the living root bridges of Meghalaya — how local communities guide tree roots across streams over many years until the roots become a strong bridge. Students look at the image and predict: 'What makes a root bridge stronger than a wooden bridge that might rot?'

In groups of three, students take two chairs separated by a gap and attempt the root bridge challenge from Textbook p. 105: build a connection using only string and sticks that can hold a small toy placed in the middle. They record in their notebooks: what they tried first, what failed, what adjustment they made, and whether the final structure held.

Groups share their strategies. Teacher asks each group: 'What was the most important change you made after your first attempt?' The class identifies common principles: tension, crossing patterns, anchoring at both ends. Teacher writes these on the board and connects them to how tree roots grow and interweave over time.

Students write a closing reflection: 'What did this challenge teach you about the way the people of Meghalaya use nature's own design?' Teacher asks: 'Could you build a root bridge quickly, or does it need something that takes time — and what is that thing?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply iterative problem-solving to a structural challenge and connect an engineering principle to a traditional practice that uses the same principle.
periods.section_context: Living root bridges, Meghalaya, string-and-stick bridge challenge, two chairs, small toy as test weight, local knowledge of root growth, Northeast India.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After the first attempt fails for most groups, pause and ask the whole class: 'What one thing would you change?' This teaches iteration as a process, not failure as an outcome. Avoid stepping in to fix — let groups discover through a second attempt.

periods.activity_title: Mapping and Exploring the Western Ghats
periods.textbook_anchor: Western Ghats — Look at the map, locate the Western Ghats and name the six states it passes through (p. 105)
materials: India physical map (from textbook or printed)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map of India showing the Western Ghats running through six states (p. 105); textbook images of lion-tailed macaque and forest (p. 105)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 105 and asks students what they already know about the word 'Ghats'. Students share ideas. Teacher then directs students to the map and asks them to trace the line of hills with their finger from north to south before writing anything.

Students work with the map from Textbook p. 105 to locate the Western Ghats and list the six states it passes through in their notebooks. They also note the names of three rivers shown originating from the Ghats (using p. 106 for the river task) and mark these on a simple outline sketch.

Students examine the forest images on Textbook pp. 105–106 and write: what animals they spot, what the people in the picture appear to be doing, and why they think forts were built on hilltops rather than on flat land. Teacher facilitates a brief pair discussion on the fort question before students write their answer.

Class discussion: Teacher asks 'Why would a chain of forested hills be the source of so many rivers?' Students reason aloud — rainfall, elevation, slow release of water — while the teacher connects their ideas to the concept of the Western Ghats as a biodiversity hotspot and water source for peninsular India.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a physical map to locate a geographic feature, trace its extent across states, and identify associated natural features such as rivers.
periods.section_context: Western Ghats, India physical map, six states, rivers originating from Western Ghats, lion-tailed macaque, Indian Giant Squirrel, forts on hilltops, tribal communities, forest images.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If the Western Ghats get heavy rain and the plains do not, where do you think the rain goes?' Guide students toward the idea of rivers and groundwater rather than giving the answer. The map tracing should be done individually before pair work begins.

periods.activity_title: Varieties Survey — Fruits, Vegetables, and Conservation
periods.textbook_anchor: Western Ghats — Pick a fruit or vegetable that grows in your state and list how many types and varieties are locally known (p. 107)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of mango varieties, citizen science survey, and Western Ghats forest (p. 107–109)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook pp. 107–108 and describes the citizen-science mango-variety survey — students, farmers, and experts working together to document how many mango varieties exist in one region. Students are asked: 'Who holds the most knowledge about local varieties — a scientist visiting once, or a farmer who has grown the tree for thirty years?' Brief open responses.

Students choose one fruit or vegetable that grows in their region and carry out the activity from Textbook p. 107: with the help of memory, classmates, or the teacher, they list as many local names and varieties of that fruit or vegetable as they can. Students compare lists in pairs, then small groups pool their lists. Teacher notes on the board the variety-counts across the class.

Class discusses: 'Where does knowledge of local varieties come from? How does it get passed down?' Teacher connects the discussion to tribal and forest-dwelling communities in the Western Ghats who have used forest plants for food and medicine across generations — and to the Save Silent Valley Movement as an example of communities acting to protect that living knowledge base.

Students write in their notebooks: three protected areas in the Western Ghats (using Textbook p. 109) and one sentence explaining what would be lost if a forest like Silent Valley were destroyed. Teacher closes: 'Whose voice mattered most in saving Silent Valley, and what does that tell you about who knows a forest best?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can document local biodiversity knowledge through a participatory survey and connect the value of that knowledge to conservation practice.
periods.section_context: Western Ghats, mango variety survey, local fruit and vegetable varieties, citizen science, tribal forest communities, medicinal plants, Save Silent Valley Movement, three protected areas.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students list varieties, accept local-language names alongside standard names — this is precisely the point. Ask: 'Did you know this variety's name from home, or did you learn it from someone here?' This surfaces the community-knowledge dimension naturally.

periods.activity_title: Vibrant India Collage — Reflecting on Four Regions
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Make a collage by pasting pictures depicting vibrant India (p. 111)
materials: Old magazines, newspapers, or printed images (brought or available in classroom)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pp. 109–111 — aquatic animal matching exercise and reflection prompts

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 110 and complete the matching exercise independently: matching aquatic animals (dolphin, turtle, sea anemone, seahorse, clownfish, starfish, jellyfish, octopus) with their distinctive features. Teacher reviews answers briefly as a class — this consolidates marine biodiversity from the Islands section.

Students respond in their notebooks to two reflection questions from Textbook p. 109: 'What surprised you most about the places visited in this journey across India and why?' and 'How is your region similar or different from one of the places in the chapter?' Students choose the question that connects most to them.

Students create a collage from Textbook p. 111 — 'Vibrant India' — using cut images, drawings, or labelled sketches that represent at least two of the four regions from the chapter. Each collage must include one natural feature and one human or cultural element per region shown. Students work individually but may share materials.

Students hold up or place their collages for a quick gallery share. Teacher invites two or three students to say one word describing what they feel about India's diversity based on what they made. Teacher closes: 'Each of these places is unique — and each one depends on people who understand and protect it.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise learning about multiple regions by selecting and combining images and ideas that represent both natural and human-cultural dimensions of a place.
periods.section_context: Aquatic animal matching (dolphin, turtle, sea anemone, seahorse, clownfish, starfish, jellyfish, octopus), reflection on four regions, region comparison, Vibrant India collage, people living in harmony with nature.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For students who do not have access to magazines, drawing and labelling is fully acceptable — make this clear at the start so no student feels at a disadvantage. Ask: 'What one thing from this chapter would you most want to tell someone who had never heard of it?'

assessment_items.question_text: Look at this description: 'It is the land where the land of India meets the sea at its southernmost point, surrounded by water on all sides.' Which of the following best matches this description?

options.label: A
options.text: Indira Point in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands

options.label: C
options.text: Lakshadweep Island in the Arabian Sea

options.label: D
options.text: The Sundarbans delta where the Ganga meets the sea

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This item assesses map-reading of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands section. Students who engaged with the map on p. 95 should distinguish Indira Point from the mainland tip at Kanyakumari.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a country-level map to locate and describe the position of natural geographic features.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses Kanyakumari — the southernmost point of the mainland — with Indira Point, which is on an island. They have not grasped the island-versus-mainland distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the two island groups of India. Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are in the Bay of Bengal. This is a sea-identification confusion from the same chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has recalled the Sundarbans as a coastal meeting point of river and sea, confusing a delta for the southernmost point. The delta is in West Bengal, not the southernmost tip.

assessment_items.question_text: A student built a paper tube and stood it on a table. It fell over. She then cut four small triangles from thick paper and attached them evenly around the bottom of the tube. This time it stood upright. Explain why the triangles helped the tube stand. Connect your answer to buttress roots.
expected_elements: The triangles spread the base of the tube outward, making it wider and more stable.
A wider base prevents the tube from tipping to one side because the weight is more evenly distributed.
Buttress roots flare out from the base of tall trees in a similar way, providing a wide support that keeps the tree upright in soft or waterlogged soil.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks if the student explains the base-widening effect AND connects it to buttress roots. Award partial marks if only one of the two parts is addressed clearly.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can test a structural hypothesis using a physical model and connect the result to a natural engineering principle.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

assessment_items.question_text: The people of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands have lived near the sea for thousands of years. When the 2004 tsunami struck, some island communities may have survived by reading signs in nature — changes in animal behaviour, the movement of water, and the sounds of the forest. Do you think this kind of knowledge is valuable? Give reasons for your answer, and explain how sea life such as coral reefs and the creatures in them might be connected to the safety and lives of people who live near the ocean.
look_for: The student recognises that long observation of the natural world builds knowledge that can predict danger (e.g., animals moving away from shore, water pulling back before a wave).
The student makes a reasoned argument for why this knowledge is valuable, not simply stating that it 'is' valuable.
The student explains at least one way coral reefs or sea creatures are connected to human life — shelter for fish that people eat, protection of coastlines, or as a sign of a healthy ocean.
The response draws a connection between protecting the ocean ecosystem and protecting the communities that depend on it.
assessment_items.annotation: This item requires reasoned evaluation, not recall. Credit any ecologically accurate connection between marine health and human wellbeing. The item is intentionally open to regional experience — students from coastal areas may draw on personal knowledge, which is valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe interdependence within a marine ecosystem and explain why protecting it matters.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

assessment_items.question_text: Mangrove trees grow in salty, waterlogged soil near the sea. Which of the following correctly explains why mangrove trees have two kinds of roots?

options.label: A
options.text: One kind of root absorbs oxygen from the air above the water; the other kind holds the soil and prevents the coastline from washing away.

options.label: B
options.text: One kind of root absorbs salt from the water; the other kind stores fresh water for the tree to use in dry weather.

options.label: C
options.text: One kind of root grows very deep to anchor the tree; the other kind spreads wide like buttress roots to make the tree stable.

options.label: D
options.text: One kind of root absorbs nutrients from the mud; the other kind floats on the surface to collect sunlight.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. Both functions must be stated for the answer to be fully correct — aerial breathing roots and soil-holding roots serve distinct purposes.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe structural features of plants and explain how those features help the plant survive in its specific habitat.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has invented a salt-filtering function not described in the chapter. This suggests they are applying general 'roots absorb things' reasoning rather than the specific observations about mangrove root types.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing mangrove roots with buttress roots from the Islands of India section. This is a cross-section confusion — both root types are wide, but their purposes and structures differ.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has invented a sunlight-collecting root function. This indicates a recall error mixed with creative inference, not engagement with the chapter's description of mangrove root functions.

assessment_items.question_text: Honey collectors in the Sundarbans wear masks on the backs of their heads when they go into the forest. Explain what problem this practice solves, and what it tells us about how the honey collectors learned about tiger behaviour.
expected_elements: Tigers tend to attack from behind, so a mask on the back of the head makes the tiger think it is being watched, deterring an attack.
The practice shows that honey collectors observed tiger behaviour carefully over a long time and discovered that tigers avoid attacking when they think they are seen.
This knowledge was built through generations of living in and depending on the Sundarbans forest.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks if the student explains the deterrence mechanism and references observation as the source of the knowledge. A response that only states the mask 'scares' tigers without explaining the behavioural basis receives partial marks.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how a community's way of life is shaped by and dependent on a specific natural ecosystem.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

assessment_items.question_text: A student is looking at pictures from a market in Northeast India. She notices bamboo stalls, colourful woven cloth, and large pots of local food. She also sees houses in the background built on tall bamboo stilts. What does this combination of features most likely tell her about the people of Northeast India?

options.label: A
options.text: They use what the forest provides — bamboo, cloth from weaving traditions, and local food — in both their everyday tools and their homes.

options.label: B
options.text: They do not have access to brick or concrete, so they use bamboo only because they have no other choice.

options.label: C
options.text: The market is near a river that floods often, which is why all buildings are made of bamboo so they can be rebuilt easily.

options.label: D
options.text: The bamboo houses are a sign that this is a poor region with few resources compared to other parts of India.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This item assesses whether students read the images as evidence of a rich, forest-integrated culture rather than as evidence of poverty or limitation.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read visual sources to identify features of a region's natural environment and cultural life, and articulate what the images reveal about human-nature relationships.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is interpreting bamboo use as a deficiency rather than as an intentional, culturally rich choice. This is a bias toward urban or industrial materials as the default 'better' option.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has invented a flood explanation not present in the section. While flooding does occur in some Northeast regions, the textbook's bamboo-house question is about structure and forest resources, not flood response specifically.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is applying a poverty narrative to a region's material culture, failing to recognise that using local forest materials reflects deep ecological knowledge and craft tradition, not deprivation.

assessment_items.question_text: During the bird nest building activity, your group chose dry grass, cotton, and thin twigs to build a nest. Another group used only thick sticks and got a heavy, rough nest. Which nest do you think is better for keeping eggs safe, and why? What does your answer tell you about what a bird needs when it builds a nest?
expected_elements: The nest with dry grass, cotton, and thin twigs is better because it is soft enough to cushion eggs and prevent them from cracking.
A good nest needs to be lightweight and flexible so it does not break fragile eggs, and warm enough to retain heat.
Birds select materials carefully based on what the nest needs to do — protect, insulate, and cushion — showing that nest-building is a purposeful, adapted behaviour.
assessment_items.annotation: The item is grounded in the nest-building activity. Full marks require both a material-based comparison and a stated principle about what a nest must do. Accept any correctly reasoned material comparison based on the activity experience.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design a simple structure to meet specific natural requirements and connect the design process to the way communities observe and protect wildlife.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

assessment_items.question_text: In the root bridge challenge, a group tried to span the gap between two chairs using only two straight sticks laid side by side. The structure collapsed when a small toy was placed on it. They then criss-crossed the sticks and added string tied in a X-pattern across the span. This time the structure held. Explain why the criss-cross design was stronger. How does this connect to the way living root bridges in Meghalaya are made?
expected_elements: The criss-cross pattern distributes the weight of the toy across more contact points rather than concentrating it on two parallel lines, reducing the chance of collapse.
Crossed and tied elements lock into each other and resist bending or sliding apart when a load is placed on them.

Living root bridges grow over many years as roots interweave, cross, and fuse — creating a similar interlocking network that becomes stronger as more roots join, which is why they can bear the weight of people.
assessment_items.annotation: Full marks require an explanation of the structural principle (load distribution or interlocking) AND the connection to root bridge growth. A response that only describes what happened without explaining why receives partial marks.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply iterative problem-solving to a structural challenge and connect an engineering principle to a traditional practice that uses the same principle.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

assessment_items.question_text: A student is looking at a physical map of India. She wants to find the Western Ghats. Which of the following correctly describes where she should look and what she will find?

options.label: A
options.text: A long chain of hills running along the western coast of India through six states, from which several major rivers begin.

options.label: B
options.text: A wide flat plain along the eastern coast of India, drained by rivers that flow into the Bay of Bengal.

options.label: C
options.text: A group of islands off the western coast of India in the Arabian Sea, known for dense forests.

options.label: D
options.text: A mountain range along the northern border of India that is the source of the Ganga and other great rivers.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This item tests map-reading and location of the Western Ghats as a geographic feature, including its role as a river source.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a physical map to locate a geographic feature, trace its extent across states, and identify associated natural features such as rivers.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused the Western Ghats with the Eastern Ghats or the coastal plains. They have not used directional cues on the map — the Western Ghats run along the WESTERN coast, not the east.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused a mainland hill range with an island group, possibly because both are in the west of India or both are forested. This is a geographic conflation error within the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the Western Ghats with the Himalayas. Both are associated with rivers, but the Himalayas are in the north. This error suggests the student recalled 'mountains → rivers' without using the map to check location.

assessment_items.question_text: During the fruit and vegetable variety survey, your class collected names of many local varieties of one fruit or vegetable — names that elders, farmers, and family members knew but that are not in any school textbook. Why do you think this kind of community knowledge matters? Use what you learned about the Western Ghats — including the mango variety survey, tribal communities, and the Save Silent Valley Movement — to explain your answer.
look_for: The student recognises that community and elder knowledge about local varieties is built over generations and cannot be easily found in written sources.
The student connects local variety knowledge to biodiversity — more varieties means more resilience, more options, and richer ecosystems.
The student references the Western Ghats as a biodiversity hotspot where tribal and forest-dependent communities have maintained this knowledge through their way of life.

The student draws a connection between community knowledge and conservation action, such as the Save Silent Valley Movement, where people who knew and depended on the forest were its most effective protectors.
The response makes an evaluative argument — not just description — about why this knowledge should be valued and preserved.
assessment_items.annotation: This item is intentionally open to regional variation. Accept any locally accurate variety names or examples. The strength of the response lies in the quality of reasoning about the relationship between community knowledge and conservation — not in which specific varieties are named.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can document local biodiversity knowledge through a participatory survey and connect the value of that knowledge to conservation practice.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

assessment_items.task: Make a 'Vibrant India' collage that shows at least TWO of the four regions you studied — Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Sundarbans, Northeast India, and Western Ghats. For each region you include, your collage must show: one natural feature (a plant, animal, landform, or ecosystem) and one way that people live with or depend on that natural feature. You may use cut pictures, your own drawings, labels, or a mix of all three.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each region I chose, I will show: (1) a natural feature — what it is and what makes it special. (2) a human connection — how people live with, use, or protect it. I will use pictures / drawings / labels to make this visible.
format_of_output: Collage on A4 or A3 paper
Each region shows one natural feature and one human-nature connection
Labels or captions identifying what is shown
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any combination of drawn, cut, or labelled elements. The key criterion is the presence of both a natural feature AND a human connection for each region shown. Students who include more than two regions should receive recognition but are not penalised for omitting detail in the additional regions.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise learning about multiple regions by selecting and combining images and ideas that represent both natural and human-cultural dimensions of a place.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The collage reveals whether the student can identify and pair natural features with human cultural or livelihood connections across different regions — showing synthesis rather than isolated recall.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts students to plan before they create. A student who uses it well will have two clear panels — one per region — each with a named natural element and a stated human connection. Look for intentionality in the pairing, not just the presence of images.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Both regions are clearly represented; natural features are correctly identified; the human connection is specific (e.g., honey collectors depend on mangroves, not just 'people live there'); labels or captions make the connection explicit. Weak: Only images are pasted without any labelling or connection drawn; one region is represented but not the other; natural features and human connections are not paired.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students without access to magazines may draw and label entirely — this is explicitly valid. Students who struggle with labelling in English may write in their home language or use symbols. The collage is a visual-synthesis task, not a writing task.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Collage (cut, drawn, or mixed media) on paper
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The collage format from Textbook p. 111 directly assesses the synthesis goal of the closing section — students must actively select, combine, and present, which requires them to judge what is most representative of each region's natural and human dimensions.
